profile.name: Papa Stour Sword Dance
profile.tagline: A seven-person linked sword dance from the Shetland Islands featuring the Champions of Christendom.
profile.insight: In 1814, Sir Walter Scott recorded a verbal description of the Papa Stour Sword Dance, a performance featuring seven dancers representing the Champions of Christendom that nearly vanished in the 19th century.
profile.profile: The Papa Stour Sword Dance is a traditional linked sword dance originating from the island of Papa Stour in Shetland. It features seven dancers representing the Seven Champions of Christendom, including figures like St. George and St. Andrew. The dance is characterized by a solo fiddle accompaniment and a structure that alternates between individual introductions and a collective reel.
profile.profile_long:
The Papa Stour Sword Dance, also known as the Shetland Sword Dance, is a distinct British linked sword dance that serves as a living historical record of the island of Papa Stour. The dance is structured around seven performers, each embodying one of the Seven Champions of Christendom: St. James of Spain, St. Denis of France, St. David of Wales, St. Patrick of Ireland, St. Anthony of Italy, St. Andrew of Scotland, and St. George of England. This performance tradition, which originated on the island of Papa Stour, faced a period of decline in the early 1800s, nearly reaching the point of extinction. Its survival is largely attributed to the interest of Sir Walter Scott, who included a fictionalized account of the dance in his 1820 novel, 'The Pirate'. Scott later provided a more detailed description and the original lyrics in the notes to the 1831 Magnum Opus edition of the same work, referring to it as a 'Danish or Norwegian Ballet.'

The musical structure of the dance is as precise as its choreography. It is performed in the key of A major, typically by a solo fiddle. The performance is divided into two primary segments: 'The Tripp' and the 'Dance Proper.' The Tripp serves as a short, introductory section in quadruple meter, providing the musical backdrop for each of the seven dancers to perform a 'pas seul.' Following these individual introductions, the Dance Proper commences. This section is described as a 'muckle reel' by Peter Cook, a key figure in the preservation of Shetland fiddle traditions. The Dance Proper is composed of three distinct sections that are repeated as necessary until the performance concludes. These sections shift in meter: the A section is in duple meter, the B section transitions to quadruple meter, and the C section moves into triple meter.

The lyrical component of the dance is equally significant. Before each repetition of the Tripp, the dancers recite verses to introduce the characters. These lyrics, which describe the origins and exploits of each champion, were documented by both Sir Walter Scott and Dr. Samuel Hibbert, the latter of whom published his own version in his 1822 work, 'Description of the Shetland Islands.' These historical scripts remain the primary reference for modern performers. The dance has undergone a series of revivals since the 19th century and continues to be practiced today. Currently, the tradition is maintained by a group of 25 members, split between junior and senior teams, ensuring that the choreography and the accompanying fiddle music remain a part of the Shetland cultural landscape. The dance is a testament to the endurance of local performance traditions, having transitioned from a near-extinct practice to a documented and actively performed piece of heritage.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated on the island of Papa Stour in the Shetland Islands. It was documented by Reverend George Low around 1770 and later by Sir Walter Scott in 1814. It was nearly extinct by the early 1800s but was preserved through the literary works of Scott and the descriptive accounts of Dr. Samuel Hibbert in 1822. The tradition has been revived multiple times since the 19th century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves seven dancers who perform in a linked formation. Each dancer performs a 'pas seul' during the introductory 'Tripp' section. The main dance, or 'Dance Proper,' follows, consisting of three repeating sections that utilize different meters. Technique not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed in the key of A major, usually by a solo fiddle. It consists of an introductory 'Tripp' in quadruple meter and a 'Dance Proper' (muckle reel) which cycles through duple, quadruple, and triple meters.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance represents the Seven Champions of Christendom. The lyrics, spoken before the Tripp, serve to introduce each character, their country of origin, and their specific exploits.
sections.notable_figures: Sir Walter Scott, Dr. Samuel Hibbert, Peter Cook, Alex Johnson.
sections.lineage: The dance is described as a 'Danish or Norwegian Ballet' in historical notes by Sir Walter Scott.

This dance dates back at least as far as 1788, but has links with Northumbrian Sword dances and the 16th century heroic characters of the 'Seven Champions of Europe' who feature in the dance.
